title: Requirements and Domain Modeling
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of requirements and domain modeling and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—functional requirements—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study requirements and domain modeling with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you keep a Java codebase understandable as its responsibilities and collaborators grow. In this lesson, focus on functional requirements and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A method gives a named contract to a unit of behavior. Keep responsibilities focused, define clear parameter and return types, and test typical, boundary, and invalid cases independently. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect functional requirements with business rules before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text: A method gives a named contract to a unit of behavior. Keep responsibilities focused, define clear parameter and return types, and test typical, boundary, and invalid cases independently.

items.title: Business rules
items.text: Maintainable design makes responsibilities, contracts, and dependency direction clear. Prefer cohesive components and focused interfaces, applying patterns and SOLID principles when they solve a real problem. Apply that reasoning specifically to business rules and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Domain entities and value objects
items.text: A class defines state and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation protects invariants by keeping mutable state private and validating updates through a small public API.

items.title: Defining invariants
items.text: Maintainable design makes responsibilities, contracts, and dependency direction clear. Prefer cohesive components and focused interfaces, applying patterns and SOLID principles when they solve a real problem. Apply that reasoning specifically to defining invariants and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Translating requirements into classes
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Separate domain decisions from input/output so logic can be tested directly. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: apply requirements and domain modeling to a small project artifact. Record the trade-off, one verification step, and a rollback or recovery path where relevant.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one listed topic from Requirements and Domain Modeling.
The learner states the expected result before running or inspecting the example.
At least one boundary, failure, compatibility, or maintainability consideration is documented where relevant.
hints: Start by identifying the contract or rule behind functional requirements.
Reduce the example to the smallest input that makes the behavior visible.
Test one boundary or failure case and compare the result with the expected behavior.
content.execution_notes: Java requires a JDK or a separate isolated server runner. No Java sandbox is bundled with this content; never execute learner code inside the FastAPI process or public production container.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.

summary: Requirements and Domain Modeling is best understood by connecting its contract to a small observable example.
Key syllabus points: Functional requirements, Business rules, Domain entities and value objects.
Use official versioned documentation and tests to confirm assumptions before relying on behavior in a larger application.
